Writing C++ Inside R with Rcpp: Faster Credit Risk Computations

R
C++
Credit Risk Analytics
Performance
Published

March 8, 2026

Introduction

R is expressive and well-suited for data science, but pure R code can become a bottleneck when you have tight loops, recursive algorithms, or iterative computations that cannot be vectorised. Parallelisation helps — but even across multiple cores you are still running R bytecode. The next lever is to drop down to C++ using the Rcpp package, which lets you write compiled functions that are called directly from R.

This tutorial walks through practical Rcpp patterns in a credit risk context, specifically accelerating the bootstrap resampling and score-scaling workflow introduced in the Score Reliability post.

By the end you will be able to:

  • Understand when Rcpp is and is not the right tool
  • Write and compile C++ functions inline and from source files
  • Use core Rcpp types (NumericVector, DataFrame, List)
  • Measure real speedups with bench::mark()

When to Reach for Rcpp

Not every slow R script needs C++. The table below summarises the decision:

Situation Better approach
Embarrassingly parallel map/apply parallel / furrr
Vectorisable arithmetic Base R / data.table
Tight loops with data-dependent branching Rcpp
Recursive algorithms Rcpp
Repeated small allocations inside a loop Rcpp
Linear algebra at scale RcppArmadillo

The key insight is that R’s interpreter overhead — function dispatch, SEXP boxing, garbage collection — is paid per operation. In a loop of one million iterations that overhead dominates. C++ pays it once at compile time.

Setup

library(Rcpp)
library(bench)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

Part 1 — Inline Functions with cppFunction()

The fastest way to experiment is cppFunction(), which compiles a single C++ function on the fly and makes it available as a regular R object.

Example 1: PDO Score Scaling

The credit-score transformation used in the reliability post applies a Points to Double the Odds (PDO) formula elementwise over a vector of log-odds predictions:

\[\text{score}_i = \alpha - \beta \cdot \text{logodds}_i, \quad \beta = \frac{PDO}{\ln 2}\]

scaling_r <- function(vec, PDO = 30, OddsAtAnchor = 2, Anchor = 700) {
  beta  <- PDO / log(2)
  alpha <- Anchor - PDO * OddsAtAnchor
  round(alpha - beta * vec, 0)
}
cppFunction('
NumericVector scaling_cpp(NumericVector vec,
                          double PDO = 30,
                          double OddsAtAnchor = 2,
                          double Anchor = 700) {
  double beta  = PDO / log(2.0);
  double alpha = Anchor - PDO * OddsAtAnchor;
  int n = vec.size();
  NumericVector out(n);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    out[i] = round(alpha - beta * vec[i]);
  }
  return out;
}
')

A few things to notice about the C++ code:

  • NumericVector is Rcpp’s equivalent of R’s numeric vector — it maps directly to R’s SEXP without copying.
  • Indexing is 0-based in C++: vec[0] is the first element.
  • The function signature mirrors what R will see: argument names and default values work the same way.
log_odds <- rnorm(1e6, mean = -2, sd = 1)

bench::mark(
  R   = scaling_r(log_odds),
  Cpp = scaling_cpp(log_odds),
  check = FALSE
)
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 R           26.14ms  26.59ms      37.0   15.26MB     74.1
2 Cpp          8.94ms   9.79ms     102.     7.63MB     28.4

For a vectorised operation like this the gap is modest — the real gains appear when we cannot vectorise.

Example 2: Winsorised Mean (Non-Vectorisable Loop)

A common risk operation is computing a winsorised (truncated) mean. The inner loop has a data-dependent branch (if v < lo), which breaks R’s vectorisation.

winsorise_mean_r <- function(x, lower = 0.01, upper = 0.99) {
  lo <- quantile(x, lower)
  hi <- quantile(x, upper)
  x  <- ifelse(x < lo, lo, ifelse(x > hi, hi, x))
  mean(x)
}
cppFunction('
double winsorise_mean_cpp(NumericVector x, double lower = 0.01, double upper = 0.99) {
  int n = x.size();

  // Sort a copy to find quantile boundaries
  NumericVector s = clone(x);
  std::sort(s.begin(), s.end());
  double lo = s[(int)(lower * (n - 1))];
  double hi = s[(int)(upper * (n - 1))];

  // Single-pass accumulation with clamping
  double total = 0.0;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    double v = x[i];
    if (v < lo) v = lo;
    if (v > hi) v = hi;
    total += v;
  }
  return total / n;
}
')
x <- rnorm(1e6)

bench::mark(
  R   = winsorise_mean_r(x),
  Cpp = winsorise_mean_cpp(x),
  check = FALSE
)
# A tibble: 2 × 6
  expression      min   median `itr/sec` mem_alloc `gc/sec`
  <bch:expr> <bch:tm> <bch:tm>     <dbl> <bch:byt>    <dbl>
1 R            49.8ms     54ms      15.0  145.22MB    56.4 
2 Cpp            50ms   50.9ms      17.9    7.63MB     1.99

The C++ version replaces three passes over the vector (quantile, ifelse × 2, mean) with one sort and one linear pass.

Part 2 — Source Files with sourceCpp()

For multi-function code, write C++ in a .cpp file. Rcpp attributes handle all the glue code automatically.

src/bootstrap_utils.cpp

// [[Rcpp::depends(Rcpp)]]
#include <Rcpp.h>
using namespace Rcpp;

// -----------------------------------------------------------------------
// Gains table computation
// Accepts a score vector and a binary event vector (0/1).
// Returns a DataFrame with decile-level event rates.
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------

// [[Rcpp::export]]
DataFrame gains_table_cpp(NumericVector scores,
                          IntegerVector events,
                          int n_bins = 10) {
  int n = scores.size();

  // Sort scores descending (high score = low risk = top decile)
  NumericVector sorted = clone(scores);
  std::sort(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), std::greater<double>());

  // Compute bin boundaries from sorted scores
  NumericVector breaks(n_bins + 1);
  for (int b = 0; b <= n_bins; b++) {
    int idx  = std::min((int)(b * (n - 1.0) / n_bins), n - 1);
    breaks[b] = sorted[idx];
  }
  breaks[0]      = sorted[0] + 1.0;        // top boundary
  breaks[n_bins] = sorted[n - 1] - 1.0;   // bottom boundary

  // Assign each observation to a bin
  IntegerVector bin_id(n, 0);
  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    for (int b = 0; b < n_bins; b++) {
      if (scores[i] <= breaks[b] && scores[i] > breaks[b + 1]) {
        bin_id[i] = b + 1;
        break;
      }
    }
  }

  // Aggregate per bin
  IntegerVector bin_n(n_bins, 0);
  IntegerVector bin_ev(n_bins, 0);
  NumericVector bin_score(n_bins, 0.0);

  for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
    int b = bin_id[i] - 1;
    if (b >= 0 && b < n_bins) {
      bin_n[b]++;
      bin_ev[b]    += events[i];
      bin_score[b] += scores[i];
    }
  }

  NumericVector event_rate(n_bins);
  for (int b = 0; b < n_bins; b++) {
    int cnt      = bin_n[b] > 0 ? bin_n[b] : 1;
    bin_score[b] /= cnt;
    event_rate[b] = (double)bin_ev[b] / cnt;
  }

  return DataFrame::create(
    Named("decile")     = seq(1, n_bins),
    Named("n")          = bin_n,
    Named("events")     = bin_ev,
    Named("event_rate") = event_rate,
    Named("mean_score") = bin_score
  );
}


// -----------------------------------------------------------------------
// Bootstrap inner loop
// pred_matrix: n_obs × n_bootstraps — each column is one replicate.
// Returns a vector of per-replicate winsorised means.
// -----------------------------------------------------------------------

// [[Rcpp::export]]
NumericVector bootstrap_winsorise_cpp(NumericMatrix pred_matrix,
                                      double lower = 0.01,
                                      double upper = 0.99) {
  int n_obs   = pred_matrix.nrow();
  int n_boots = pred_matrix.ncol();
  NumericVector result(n_boots);

  for (int b = 0; b < n_boots; b++) {
    NumericVector col = pred_matrix.column(b);
    NumericVector s   = clone(col);
    std::sort(s.begin(), s.end());

    double lo = s[(int)(lower * (n_obs - 1))];
    double hi = s[(int)(upper * (n_obs - 1))];

    double total = 0.0;
    for (int i = 0; i < n_obs; i++) {
      double v = col[i];
      if (v < lo) v = lo;
      if (v > hi) v = hi;
      total += v;
    }
    result[b] = total / n_obs;
  }

  return result;
}

Compile and load with:

sourceCpp("src/bootstrap_utils.cpp")

The // [[Rcpp::export]] attribute is the only annotation needed — Rcpp’s build system generates the R wrapper automatically.

Part 3 — End-to-End Benchmark: Bootstrap Score Reliability

We replicate the bootstrap inner loop from the Score Reliability post and compare the pure-R apply approach against the compiled C++ version.

Simulate predictions

set.seed(42)
n_obs        <- 5000
n_bootstraps <- 200

# Each column is one bootstrap replicate's log-odds predictions
pred_matrix <- matrix(
  rnorm(n_obs * n_bootstraps, mean = -2, sd = 1.2),
  nrow = n_obs,
  ncol = n_bootstraps
)

Pure-R baseline

bootstrap_winsorise_r <- function(pred_matrix, lower = 0.01, upper = 0.99) {
  apply(pred_matrix, 2, function(col) {
    lo  <- quantile(col, lower)
    hi  <- quantile(col, upper)
    col <- ifelse(col < lo, lo, ifelse(col > hi, hi, col))
    mean(col)
  })
}

Benchmark

bm <- bench::mark(
  R   = bootstrap_winsorise_r(pred_matrix),
  Cpp = bootstrap_winsorise_cpp(pred_matrix),
  check    = FALSE,
  iterations = 20
)

autoplot(bm) +
  labs(
    title    = "R vs C++ — Bootstrap winsorised means",
    subtitle = paste0(n_obs, " obs x ", n_bootstraps, " bootstrap replicates"),
    x = "Implementation",
    y = "Time"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Typical results on a single core:

Implementation Median time Speedup
R (apply + ifelse) ~380 ms 1×
C++ (bootstrap_winsorise_cpp) ~28 ms ~14×

The speedup compounds when the bootstrap runs inside an outer loop over score bands or hyperparameter grids.

Part 4 — Rcpp Types Quick Reference

R type Rcpp type Notes
numeric NumericVector Double precision
integer IntegerVector
logical LogicalVector
character CharacterVector Slower; avoid in hot loops
list List Heterogeneous container
data.frame DataFrame Wraps named vectors
matrix (numeric) NumericMatrix Column-major access is fastest

Memory note: Rcpp vectors are views into R’s memory by default — no copy. Use clone() only when you need to sort or mutate without affecting the original R object.

Common Pitfalls

Off-by-one indexing — R is 1-based; C++ is 0-based. Writing vec[1] expecting the first element (vec[0]) is the most frequent Rcpp bug.

Integer overflow — IntegerVector uses 32-bit signed integers. For large accumulations (n > 2^31) use double or long long.

NA handling — R’s NA is not C++ NaN. Use NumericVector::is_na(x[i]) to test for NA in a loop rather than comparing to NA_real_.

Unnecessary cloning — clone() copies memory. Only use it when you genuinely need an independent copy.

When Not to Use Rcpp

  • Prototyping — the compile-edit cycle is slower than pure R iteration. Profile first with profvis::profvis() and only drop to C++ after confirming the bottleneck.
  • Already vectorised code — dplyr, data.table, and base R vectorised operations are near-C speed for column-wise operations. Rewriting them in Rcpp rarely helps.
  • WebR — compiled C++ cannot run in a browser. If the WebR Playground matters, keep a pure-R fallback and show pre-computed Rcpp results alongside it.

Key Takeaways

  • cppFunction() is the quickest entry point for a single C++ function called from R.
  • sourceCpp() is the production pattern: write .cpp files annotated with // [[Rcpp::export]] and compile on demand.
  • Rcpp types (NumericVector, DataFrame, NumericMatrix) map one-to-one to R types with zero-copy semantics where possible.
  • The biggest wins come from replacing non-vectorisable loops — branch-heavy inner loops, recursive functions, iterative algorithms — not from rewriting already-vectorised R code.
  • In a bootstrap-heavy credit risk workflow a 10–15× speedup is realistic, turning a multi-minute sensitivity analysis into a near-interactive one.
